title: A Hacker Targeted High-Stakes Poker Players With Malware That Exposed Their Cards
gist: A patient threat actor compromised the multi-table poker tools Jurojin and IntuitiveTables via a software supply-chain attack, covertly installing the MeshAgent remote-access tool on a targeted list of high-stakes players to see their cards, allegedly stealing $1.5M-$4M on GGPoker and ACR alone. The scheme was discovered by a player's Claude AI agent, and operator responses diverged sharply: CoinPoker and ClubWPT Gold banned and refunded, GGPoker announced fixes after ignoring reports, and ACR denied wrongdoing and refused refunds.

insights.claim: The attacker compromised Jurojin's own software-update system and pushed a remote-access agent to existing users through normal automatic updates.
insights.speaker: WolfSec
insights.so_what: Trusted auto-update channels remain a top vector; signing and update infrastructure of small vendors is the weak link.
insights.quote: In the case of Jurojin, the attacker gained access to the developer’s own system for software updates and was able to deliver the remote-access agent to existing users through normal, automatic updates.
insights.locator: In the case of Jurojin

insights.claim: The IntuitiveTables developer was infected through a compromised Jurojin update on a test machine, letting the attacker inject malicious code before the developer signed an official build, so the backdoor shipped as a legitimate signed public download.
insights.speaker: WolfSec
insights.so_what: Chained supply-chain compromise: one vendor's breach cascades into another's code signing, defeating signature-based trust.
insights.quote: Using the agent, the attacker added malicious code to the Intuitive Tables application before the developer signed the security certificate for an updated build of the app.
insights.locator: The developer of Intuitive Tables

insights.claim: Because the malware arrived via standard update channels or official releases, neither users nor their antivirus software detected anything.
insights.speaker: Ben Dowsett
insights.so_what: Endpoint AV is blind to signed supply-chain payloads; behavioral monitoring is required.
insights.quote: In both instances, the malicious code was delivered through a standard update channel or an official release, so neither the users nor their antivirus apps detected anything amiss.

insights.claim: The trojanized tool checked local usernames against a hard-coded target list hosted on attacker infrastructure and only behaved maliciously for listed players, otherwise acting as the normal program.
insights.speaker: WolfSec
insights.so_what: Targeted, conditional payloads minimize detection footprint and make sandbox analysis less effective.
insights.quote: If you weren’t on that list, then it became the normal program and didn’t do anything malicious at all.
insights.locator: If you were on a hard-coded list

insights.claim: Malicious software was pushed to an estimated more than a thousand users of the two multi-table applications, with hundreds of players allegedly targeted over multiple years.
insights.speaker: WolfSec
insights.so_what: Niche professional tools can carry outsized blast radius in high-value user communities.
insights.quote: The hacker compromised both applications, WolfSec says, pushing malicious software to over a thousand estimated users.
insights.locator: Instead of targeting individual players directly

insights.claim: Unlike typical financially motivated actors who immediately drain wallets after gaining access, this attacker left large crypto holdings on victims' machines untouched and focused on long-term reconnaissance and card-viewing.
insights.speaker: WolfSec
insights.so_what: Absence of theft is not absence of compromise; patient actors monetize information advantage rather than direct theft.
insights.quote: they’ll hit everyone all at once and dump all the wallets

insights.claim: The same threat actor is believed to have attempted attacks on players' machines as early as 2022 with a more basic technique; because no funds were stolen, no further action was taken after players wiped the malware.
insights.speaker: WolfSec
insights.so_what: Failed or quiet early intrusions are signals of a returning actor and should trigger deeper investigation.
insights.locator: But this hacker didn’t do any of that

insights.claim: The cheating account played disciplined, standard bet sizes and normal hand ranges so that individual sessions looked unremarkable; only its long-run win rate drew scrutiny.
insights.speaker: Mike (pseudonymous pro player)
insights.so_what: Statistical anomaly detection over long samples, not session-level review, is the main defense against perfect-information cheating.
insights.quote: Its session-by-session play never raised too many eyebrows; only the account’s win rate over time drew scrutiny.

insights.claim: The alleged cheater operated across several sites under multiple handles, including JackKlompus on ACR, Europe on CoinPoker, OxOO, and another handle on ClubWPT Gold, refusing to identify themselves in table chat.
insights.speaker: Ben Dowsett
insights.so_what: Cross-site identity sharing among operators would materially shorten cheater lifetimes.

insights.claim: A professional player's Claude AI agent, while reviewing play statistics after a database crash, noticed MeshAgent running in the background and identified 11 time-stamped screen-capture events, 10 of which coincided with the same opponent at his ACR table.
insights.speaker: Ben Dowsett
insights.so_what: General-purpose AI agents with system access are emerging as ad hoc endpoint-security tools for individuals.
insights.quote: In a fitting sign of the times, the hacker’s carefully laid plans were foiled by an AI agent.
insights.locator: In a fitting sign of the times

insights.claim: MeshAgent had been installed on the victim's machine on April 24, months before discovery on September 25, 2026.
insights.speaker: Ben Dowsett
insights.so_what: Dwell times of five months illustrate how long covert remote access can persist undetected on prosumer machines.
insights.locator: Thanks to the Claude agent’s report

insights.claim: The hacker remained active on GGPoker and ACR until late September 2026, allegedly stealing between $1.5 million and $4 million based on source estimates.
insights.speaker: Ben Dowsett
insights.so_what: Operator inaction translates directly into player losses and potential liability/reputational exposure.

insights.claim: CoinPoker identified the player via a webcam security interview in February 2025, banned them, and refunded over $100,000, with refunds delayed months because the cheater appealed to regulators; it says ACR ignored its findings.
insights.speaker: Mario Mosböck
insights.so_what: Proactive banning on statistical evidence alone is feasible and earns player trust.
insights.locator: This alleged cheater’s presence in online circles

insights.claim: A coach reported three-to-four standard deviation outliers to GGPoker in early September 2026 but received no response until after the public reveal, when the site said there wasn't conclusive evidence.
insights.speaker: Patrick Howard
insights.so_what: Integrity teams that require proof of mechanism rather than statistical evidence leave windows for sustained theft.

insights.claim: Players had been reporting the cheater for about a year and some platforms completely ignored them.
insights.speaker: John Andress
insights.so_what: Anti-cheat vendors see a gap between operator incentives and integrity enforcement; a market for third-party integrity services.
insights.quote: Players are frustrated, because they had been reporting this for a year
insights.locator: Players are frustrated

insights.claim: GGPoker announced on October 15 that it will ban third-party tools, add win-rate anomaly detection, and has traced the attacker's funds to a Coinbase account it asked to be restricted.
insights.speaker: Ben Dowsett
insights.so_what: Banning third-party tools reshapes the professional multi-tabling ecosystem and the vendors built on it.
insights.locator: To its credit, GGPoker acknowledged

insights.claim: ACR told players on October 18 it found no compromised game outcomes and will issue no refunds, while in the same email announcing a feature to block remote-viewing tools from capturing card images.
insights.speaker: Ben Dowsett
insights.so_what: Contradictory messaging signals liability avoidance and risks eroding high-stakes player trust in ACR.
insights.quote: But ACR is going the opposite direction
insights.locator: But ACR is going the opposite direction

insights.claim: The sites themselves must ban suspicious players; the author's sources argue operators dropped the ball and that defenses only work if sites act before, not after, major attacks.
insights.speaker: Patrick Howard
insights.so_what: Online poker integrity is an operator-governance problem; regulatory or reputational pressure may follow.
insights.quote: Ultimately, the sites have to ban the players

insights.claim: Superuser cheating, where a cheater sees opponents' hole cards, has precedents including Absolute Poker and Ultimate Bet in the mid-2000s and a 2013 stolen-laptop malware case, but online poker had gone years without a confirmed incident before this one.
insights.speaker: Ben Dowsett
insights.so_what: The threat has shifted from insider site access to endpoint compromise of players.
insights.locator: Two major sites in online poker’s early days

insights.claim: Community responses included detection tools from Jurojin and IntuitiveTables, an open-source superuser detection tool from A5 Labs' AceGuardian, and a complaint to the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center.
insights.speaker: Ben Dowsett
insights.so_what: Open-source integrity tooling may become a baseline expectation across poker sites.
insights.locator: Other entities have taken concrete action
